title: Movable type was invented in China 400 years before Gutenberg
body: Around the 1040s, a Chinese artisan named Bi Sheng made individual characters from fired clay that could be arranged, printed and reused. We know of him only because the scholar Shen Kuo described the method in his Dream Pool Essays. Yet woodblock printing stayed dominant in China for centuries, partly because a full set of type for a script with thousands of characters was costly to make and sort.

slides.heading: Earliest first
items: The Jikji, printed with metal type
slides.explanation: Bi Sheng’s clay type dates from the 1040s, Wang Zhen’s wooden type from around 1300, the Jikji from 1377 and Gutenberg’s Bible from the 1450s.

slides.heading: Clay, then wood
slides.text: The Chinese artisan Bi Sheng tried wooden type but dropped it, since wood grain and soaked-up ink made it uneven. Around 1300 the official Wang Zhen made wooden type work.

slides.heading: Korea goes metal
slides.text: In 1377 a Korean Buddhist temple printed the Jikji with movable metal type, the oldest surviving book of its kind. One volume is now in the National Library of France.

slides.heading: Gutenberg’s edge
slides.text: His Bible appeared in the 1450s, 78 years after the Jikji. An alphabet of a few dozen letters, plus a press and oil-based ink, made reusable type cheap.

slides.heading: Four centuries of movable type
slides.note: Bi Sheng worked in the 1040s and Gutenberg’s Bible appeared in the 1450s; the marks sit mid-decade.

slides.heading: Who made what?
slides.explanation: Bi Sheng’s clay type is known only from Shen Kuo’s Dream Pool Essays; Wang Zhen made wooden type work around 1300; Gutenberg printed his Bible in the 1450s.
